newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African business sees soft-landing for economy.
newsitem.headline: S.African business sees soft-landing for economy.

text.p: The cushioning effects of a buoyant manufacturing sector and lower interest rates will guide South Africa's economy to a soft-landing this year, the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said on Tuesday.

"The resilience of the manufacturing sector is likely to be the stabilising factor in the economy this year, given the sudden fall in the gold price and that the agricultural sector is unlikely to match last year's growth," director general Raymond Parsons told a news briefing.
"Growth in the real economy will also be supported by the likely reduction in interest rates towards the latter part of the year," he added.
Gross domestic product data for the first quarter showed aggregate output growth of 2.4 percent, mainly on the back of strong manufacturing output.
"This is in keeping with the consensus view that the economy will growth by 2-2.5 percent this year," Parsons said.

The chamber attributed the 3.5 percent rise in manufacturing output in the first quarter to export demand. And its monthly survey of manufacturers showed that export demand was expected to increase in the year ahead.
Exports in the year to May grew by 20 percent -- outpacing import growth of around 14 percent.
"This suggests that export demand for manufacturers will continue to play a positive role in boosting production at a time when domestic demand is cooling off," it said.
Sacob said there were a number of factors which suggested that there was scope for a reduction in interest rates later in the year.

These were the general acceptance that inflation had peaked; higher gold and foreign exchange reserves; positive financial market reaction to the July 1 removal of foreign exchange controls; and an expected reduction in private sector credit extension.
"These factors suggest that conditions are appropriate to allow the Reserve Bank to reduce the Bank rate.
"Sacob believes that there is enough scope for a two percentage point decline in the prime rate over the next few months."
Parsons said he expected the first interest rate reduction to be considered on or before the Reserve Bank's annual meeting in late August.
The chamber said lower interest rates would go a long way towards restoring internal consumer confidence and lay a foundation for a better growth performance next year.
